tweet_summary: Retells the 2017 story of 7-year-old Matilda Jones finding a 4-foot sword in Cornwall's Dozmary Pool, the lake legend associates with King Arthur's Excalibur.
why_note_decision: The tweet recounts a real, well-documented 2017 event and only invokes the Excalibur connection as 'according to legend' — i.e. a framing flourish, not a factual claim that the sword is Excalibur. Mark Wilkins's reenactment-sword origin (1980s) is a charming side fact but the tweet doesn't assert otherwise. The original note debunks a claim the tweet didn't make and the Plymouth/Cornwall Live links it cites confirm the underlying find is genuine.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The tweet retells a real 2017 news story and uses 'according to legend' framing about Excalibur, not a sincere factual claim. Any note that 'corrects' the legend framing, that says the sword isn't Excalibur, or that surfaces the Mark Wilkins reenactment-sword origin as if it contradicts the tweet, is a false positive. The presence of the sword, the girl, and the discovery are all true.

original_unhelpful_note.text: The sword's owner, Mark Wilkins, identified it as his "Flambard Fantasy" reenactment blade that he threw into the pool in the 1980s as an offering, not a film prop. https://www.plymouthherald.co.uk/news/local-news/king-arthur-sword-found-lake-438667 https://www.cornwalllive.com/news/cornwall-news/the-king-arthur-sword-not-443411
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: Note 'corrects' a claim (that it's a film prop / that it's Excalibur) the tweet never makes; tweet only invokes the Arthurian lake as legend. Note adds trivia but no correction is warranted.

fact_check.notes: 2017 Matilda Jones find at Dozmary Pool is real. Sword was a modern reenactment piece thrown in by Mark Wilkins in the 1980s; tweet doesn't claim it is Excalibur, only that the lake is the legendary Excalibur location, which matches Cornish folklore.

importance.lens_rationale: Light folklore retelling on a non-political topic; little EA/progress/safety relevance. Mainly informs taxonomy of false-positive notes.
